A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same LARP framework and share identifiable methods, experiments, and theoretical results. All 24 pages of v1 and 34 pages of v4, including appendices, were readable; figures and equations could be checked visually.

before.justification: v1 reports original Gaussian mean-estimation simulations and Adult/CIFAR-10 experiments, including learner-specific results and supplementary analyses in Appendix C.

after.justification: v4 reports original experiments throughout Section 5 and Appendix D, including retained studies and new BAF, CIFAR-10N, Tiny ImageNet, and filtering comparisons.

M1.justification: The original minimax framework remains, but v4 adds learner-specific accuracy/fairness objectives and integrates subgroup sampling controlled by three parameters (Section 5.2, Algorithm 2). Section 4.2 also introduces an oracle filter parameterized by removal fraction and effectiveness. These extend the objectives and procedures; Algorithm 1 primarily formalizes existing filtering.

E1.justification: v4 adds CIFAR-10N with human annotation errors, Tiny ImageNet with 200 image classes, and BAF fraud classification with fairness objectives (Section 5.2; Appendices D.3 and D.6). Adult and CIFAR-10 label-noise and shortcut coverage remain, with shortcut experiments moved to the appendix.

E2.justification: v4 Table 1 adds evaluated Confident Learning-based and oracle filters alongside the default filter. Figure 5a adds a no-prefiltering comparator to the Gaussian experiment, absent from v1 Figure 1a. The quantile, z-score, SDO, and earlier alternative shortcut filters remain.

E3.justification: Adult changes from 14 tuned robust/brittle model instances to seven models using library defaults and a fixed neural-network configuration; its label-noise metric changes from accuracy to macro-F1. New protocols include a wider CNN and different regularization range for Tiny ImageNet, and seven Random Forest learners with different fairness weights for BAF.

E4.justification: v4 adds sensitivity analyses for oracle effectiveness and Confident Learning-based filtering, and extends learner-diameter analysis to label noise (Appendices D.4, D.5, D.8). Existing shortcut diameter, alternative-filter, and loss-reweighting studies are retained. The original default-filter learner-specific shortcut profiles in v1 Figures 6 and 7b are omitted.

E5.justification: Both versions specify eight repetitions and standard errors for Gaussian mean estimation, and repeated-run averages with error bars for classification. v4 extends uncertainty reporting to new comparisons, including Table 1, without introducing a changed run count, seed policy, or statistical testing procedure.

E6.justification: v4 adds substantial benchmark and filter-comparison results. For example, Table 1 reports CIFAR-10 high-heterogeneity prices of 2.2% (s.e. 0.2) for default filtering and 2.0% (s.e. 0.2) for CL-based filtering. Adult results are replaced under revised settings. Gaussian-risk values and the plotted quantile/z-score ordering also change between v1 Figure 1a and v4 Figure 5a without an explained protocol change.

T1.justification: The Gaussian/Huber-contamination result becomes a theorem for strictly smooth distributions under strong contamination, retaining the Gaussian bound as Corollary 4.5. v4 adds the oracle PAC-style Theorem 4.6 and general utility conditions in Corollary 5.2, replacing v1's mean-specific Appendix D argument. The original cost-sharing lemma is retained as Theorem 5.1.

C1.justification: v1 emphasizes scalar Gaussian mean estimation and algorithm heterogeneity. v4 explicitly claims feasibility in two theoretical settings and adds heterogeneous downstream risk functions as a contribution. Its abstract frames large-dataset benefits more cautiously as potential savings in repeated curation within a cost-sharing model.

C2.justification: v4 adds explanations for nonmonotonic dependence on contamination and filter effectiveness, and conjectures why Tiny ImageNet shows a weaker price signal. It expands the applicability discussion for cost-sharing conditions and identifies sample modification, particularly token editing in language modeling, as outside the current sample-removal framework.

D1.justification: v4 adds a stated public code link, filtering pseudocode, and model/scoring-function mappings in Appendix E. It documents new experimental configurations, replaces Adult tuning tables with defaults and neural-network settings, and revises reported GPU usage from 200 to 250 hours. Appendix G expands dataset access/licensing information and changes the CIFAR-10 license statement.

R1.justification: Section 2 adds substantive comparisons with distributionally robust optimization, multi-distribution learning, and the price of robustness. Appendix E connects LARP's filtering structure to LAION and C4 curation. New Confident Learning and fairness references support additional methodological relationships; the original first-framework novelty claim remains.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion are substantially rewritten. Theory is reorganized with major proofs in the main text; Gaussian experiments and shortcut descriptions move into Appendix D. The supplementary material is extensively restructured, and new algorithm and applicability discussions reshape the narrative beyond simple renumbering.

P2.justification: v1's twelve-panel Figure 2 is split and rearranged into v4 Figures 2 and 6. Selected learner-specific plots move into main-text Figure 1, while new comparison tables, benchmark plots, sensitivity plots, and pseudocode displays are added. Adult hyperparameter tables and some shortcut profiles disappear, alongside extensive journal-format layout changes.

improvement.justification: v4 substantially strengthens support for LARP's generality beyond v1's narrow theoretical setting and synthetic-corruption benchmarks. Broader guarantees, natural annotation errors, alternative filters, and conflicting fairness objectives test important aspects of the central argument. Explicit cost-sharing conditions, pseudocode, and a stated code release also improve scrutiny and reproducibility. Unexplained Gaussian-result revisions and omitted shortcut profiles limit parts of the evidence, but do not outweigh these substantial gains.
